title: Science and knowledge

paragraphs.text: If one were to compare the images seen by an 11th-century philosopher and a present-day physicist looking out over the countryside in any European country, there would be little to differentiate them – power lines and distant motorways apart. But the differences in how they made sense of what they saw would be vast. The meaning of the world stretching out before them would depend upon the conceptual scheme each used as the filter, organiser and interpreter of their experience. Both schemes would be beautiful, rich and immensely complex; both would be in many ways strange and powerful. But the scheme of the present-day physicist is incomparably stranger and more powerful, because whereas the source of the 11th-century philosopher's vision would have been largely imaginative and subjective, the source of the modern physicist's vision is intellectual and objective.

Over the centuries, science has transformed mankind's self-understanding and relationship to the world. The popular science books that now abound permit everyone to become familiar with advances in biological science, fundamental physics, and other fields that attract public attention. This is positive; the more scientifically literate the world becomes the better. However, today scientific illiteracy is widespread, and the major reason for that is usually attributed to science's sheer complexity. Non-scientists find it difficult to comprehend, and the consequent ignorance is the source of mistrust and fear. To many, science now seems to promise frightening, unknown consequences of genetic engineering, pollutions of various kinds, and other unforeseeable dangers. An extraordinary anti-scientific coalition of people has arisen, consisting of some who are ignorant of science, and others who correctly understand only too well the bad uses that it can be turned to.

Defenders of science argue that the intention of science is not to threaten human interests, to pose environmental danger or to view the world negatively. Instead they affirm the progressive and liberating aspects of science, and say that if these were better understood there would be no damaging divide between what the philosopher C P Snow labelled the 'two cultures' (that is, the cultures of science and of the humanities). Proponents of science are particularly concerned to show that most fears expressed by science's enemies are misplaced, arguing that science actually provides the remedy for the difficulties it sometimes creates, and that it will continue to generate benefits as it progresses, just as it has in the past.

No doubt this response is largely right. Most applications of science are beneficial: consider electric lights, medical technology, microchips, air travel, and much else. But scientist and non-scientist alike must acknowledge that there can be problems, such as the dangers caused by radioactive fallout from nuclear accidents, and the disasters that might accrue from mistakes in genetic manipulation. One can be a strong supporter of science without covering up risk or making unconvincing excuses. And one can still say that little in human history compares with the magnificence of science, or the power and truth of the scientific method.

Under the accepted rules of that method, a researcher proceeds by subjecting a hypothesis to rigorous examination, wherever possible experimentally in an effort to prove the hypothesis false. If the hypothesis does not turn out to be wrong, then the theory stands for the time being. However, failure to prove a theory false does not mean the theory is actually true, only that it can be used until something better appears. Accordingly all science must be continually defended; further and stronger evidence can always refute or change it. The essence of science is healthy scepticism and open-mindedness.

Of course, science does have its limitations. Each branch of science is concerned with a defined range of phenomena. Botanists, geologists and meteorologists study plants, rocks and weather respectively. No branch tries to explain the achievements of the Renaissance Italian artist Michelangelo (1475-1564) or the ethical dimension, say, of political choices. These matters – art and politics – are subjects for debate themselves, and no scientist would presume that answers to the problems they pose can be discovered by science. Critics of science, however, have a vague and certainly mistaken notion that this latter is what, in fact, scientists aspire to. This leads some critics to accuse scientists of getting involved in issues where it is inappropriate for them to do so, and others to complain when science fails to address such issues. Both criticisms reflect a hopeless ignorance of what is being attacked.

All things considered, the achievements of science have been truly heroic. Time and again, it has forced us to reconsider what are thought to be basic truths, and to learn to overcome the intellectual challenges that that reconsideration poses. In the early 20th century, the Austrian physicist Ludwig Boltzmann proclaimed that the new and then oftentimes dangerous field of aviation needed genius-heroes. He was right: it took heroism to risk one's life in the fragile aircraft that first ventured into the skies, and it required genius to discover and apply the rules of aerodynamics to building those strange-looking flying machines. Within a few years ordinary people became aviators, who for their own self-interest in the air learned things like the angle of glide as well as any physicist. But scientists today continue to be heroes and geniuses. They are most often quiet heroes and unknown geniuses, but their accomplishments continue to be breathtaking.
